title: Who decides what's good?
html:
The evidence-based approach has a possible blind spot that is about power and knowledge, not measurement.

GiveWell co-founder Holden Karnofsky called it the “white in shining armor” fallacy: the rich-world donor as the hero who fixes problems for passive beneficiaries. Outsiders often understand local conditions poorly, and trying to solve problems we don’t understand can make things worse. Most progress has to be driven locally, so the question becomes what outsiders can usefully help with. Three responses:

  • Stick to comparative advantage. Karnofsky helps his friends with computer problems, where he knows something, and not with choosing clothes. The track record suggests health and nutrition are where outside funders help most reliably. They are not the only important problems, but they can be worked on from a distance.

  • Give cash. GiveDirectly puts the decisions in recipients' hands, and the evidence consistently shows they spend the money well.

  • Acknowledge the limits. Even asking what recipients prefer involves outsiders framing the question. Alongside “does this work?”, ask “are we the right people to be doing this?”

Read: Holden Karnofsky, How not to be a “white in shining armor” (10 mins).
